methodBriefing.name: Self-explanation

activities.label: Membrane model
activities.title: Membrane structure and movement
activities.body: Review the model and note the key relationship. Then move to the explanation prompt.

essentialIdeas: Phospholipid bilayers are selectively permeable because hydrophobic tails block most polar or charged molecules while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily.
Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient without cellular energy, while active transport uses energy to move substances against the gradient.

activities.label: Explain in your own words
activities.title: Why membranes are selective
activities.body: Explain the membrane model in your own words. Keep it to the two main ideas.
activities.concept: Why the bilayer is selectively permeable and how transport differs by energy use and gradient
activities.correctAnswer: The phospholipid bilayer is selectively permeable because the hydrophobic interior blocks most polar or charged substances, while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily. Passive transport moves down a concentration gradient without energy, and active transport uses energy to move against the gradient.
activities.feedback: A complete answer names the hydrophobic barrier, the molecules it blocks or lets through more easily, and the energy difference between passive and active transport.

activities.label: Repair the explanation
activities.title: Fix the missing part
activities.body: Compare your answer with the model and correct any missing cause or energy detail.
activities.misconceptionSummary: The membrane works like a simple open fence, so any molecule can cross if it is small enough.
activities.concept: Correct the idea that small size alone controls crossing
activities.correctAnswer: Small size alone is not enough. The phospholipid bilayer has a hydrophobic interior that lets small nonpolar molecules cross more easily but blocks most polar or charged molecules unless transport proteins help.
activities.feedback: The repair should replace the open-fence idea with the hydrophobic barrier and the role of transport proteins.

activities.label: Explain again
activities.title: Say it again clearly
activities.body: Give a second explanation from memory. Use new wording, not the model's phrasing.
activities.concept: Independent explanation of membrane selectivity and transport energy
activities.correctAnswer: The phospholipid bilayer is selectively permeable because its hydrophobic core makes it harder for most polar or charged molecules to cross, while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily. Passive transport does not use energy and goes down a gradient, while active transport uses energy to move against a gradient.
activities.feedback: This check looks for a fresh, accurate explanation that still includes the barrier, the gradient, and the energy difference.

activities.label: Transport recognition check
activities.title: Choose the transport type
activities.body: Pick the best answer for the example. One choice is correct.
activities.concept: Classify a transport example as passive or active
choices: A substance moves from high concentration to low concentration without energy.
A substance moves from low concentration to high concentration using energy.
A substance crosses only because the membrane is made of phospholipids.
A substance moves only when the cell releases water.
activities.correctAnswer: A substance moves from low concentration to high concentration using energy.
activities.feedback: Active transport requires energy and moves against the concentration gradient; passive transport moves down the gradient without energy.

activities.label: Wrap-up
activities.title: Quick reflection
activities.body: Name one part of today's model that changed or sharpened your thinking.

targetAssignments.essentialIdea: Phospholipid bilayers are selectively permeable because hydrophobic tails block most polar or charged molecules while small nonpolar molecules pass more easily.
Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient without cellular energy, while active transport uses energy to move substances against the gradient.

items.essentialIdea: Phospholipids form a hydrophobic core that blocks most polar or charged substances.

check.title: Phospholipid barrier
check.prompt: How does phospholipid structure make the membrane selectively permeable?
check.referenceAnswer: Their hydrophilic heads face water while hydrophobic tails face inward, creating a core that resists most polar and charged molecules.
check.feedback: The key is the hydrophobic interior, not the outer heads.

items.essentialIdea: Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient without ATP; active transport uses ATP against it.

check.title: Compare transport types
check.prompt: How do passive transport and active transport differ in energy use and direction?
check.referenceAnswer: Passive transport moves down a concentration gradient without ATP, while active transport requires energy to move against a gradient.
check.feedback: The main contrast is both energy use and movement relative to the gradient.

recognitionCheck.title: Transport direction check
recognitionCheck.prompt: Which statement best describes active transport?
choices: It moves substances down their concentration gradient without ATP.
It moves substances against their concentration gradient using ATP.
It moves only water across the membrane by diffusion.
It always uses channel proteins and no energy.
recognitionCheck.correctAnswer: It moves substances against their concentration gradient using ATP.
recognitionCheck.feedback: Active transport requires energy and moves against the gradient.

activities.label: model
activities.title: Product Rule Pattern
activities.body: Study the example and note the pattern. Then answer the next prompt.

essentialIdeas: Each term comes from differentiating one factor while the other factor stays unchanged

activities.label: guided practice
activities.title: Spot the Two Parts
activities.body: Which part is being differentiated in each term? Answer in one sentence.
activities.concept: Each term comes from differentiating one factor while the other factor stays unchanged
activities.correctAnswer: One term differentiates the first factor while the second factor stays unchanged, and the other term differentiates the second factor while the first factor stays unchanged.
activities.feedback: A complete answer names both terms and which factor changes in each one. If you only mention the final formula, repair by saying what stays unchanged in each term.

activities.label: independent practice
activities.title: Use the Rule Alone
activities.body: Write the derivative of a product on your own.
activities.feedback: Correct if you wrote the product rule with one derivative term for each factor. If you wrote only one term, repair by checking both factors separately.

activities.label: recognition check
activities.title: Choose the Product Rule
activities.body: Pick the correct rule from the choices.
choices: (fg)' = f'g + fg'
(fg)' = f'g' + f'g
(fg)' = fg'
(fg)' = f'g - fg'
activities.feedback: The product rule has one term for differentiating the first factor and one term for differentiating the second factor. The other choices leave out a term or use the wrong sign.

targetAssignments.essentialIdea: Each term comes from differentiating one factor while the other factor stays unchanged

items.essentialIdea: The product rule states (fg)' equals f'g plus fg'.

check.title: State the product rule
check.prompt: What is the derivative of the product fg?
check.referenceAnswer: (fg)' = f'g + fg'. It adds the derivative of f times g and f times the derivative of g.
check.feedback: Both factors contribute one term; do not collapse them into one derivative.

items.essentialIdea: Differentiating a product gives one term from f and one term from g.

check.title: Where product terms come from
check.prompt: Why does differentiating fg produce two terms?
check.referenceAnswer: Because each factor can vary while the other is held unchanged, giving f'g and fg'.
check.feedback: The two terms come from changing each factor separately, not from repeating the same derivative twice.

recognitionCheck.title: Identify the product rule
recognitionCheck.prompt: Which rule correctly differentiates a product fg?
choices: (fg)' = f'g + fg'
(fg)' = f'g'
(fg)' = f + g
(fg)' = fg
recognitionCheck.feedback: The correct rule has two terms, one for each factor.

activities.label: Product rule model
activities.title: Product rule structure
activities.body: Study the rule map, then get ready to explain it back in your own words.

essentialIdeas: Differentiate a product by using the product rule on the two function factors.

activities.label: Explain product rule
activities.title: State the product rule
activities.body: Write the rule in your own words. Then compare it with the model.
activities.correctAnswer: When differentiating a product of two functions, take the derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second.
activities.feedback: A complete answer names both terms and shows that both factors stay involved. If you left out one term, repair by naming the two parts separately.

activities.label: Repair product rule
activities.title: Fix the product step
activities.body: Correct the missing step, then restate the rule once more.
activities.misconceptionSummary: Differentiating a product means differentiating each factor separately and adding the results.
activities.correctAnswer: Differentiate one factor, keep the other factor unchanged, then add the second factor differentiated with the first unchanged.
activities.feedback: The error is treating the two factors as if they were independent sums. The correct rule keeps both original factors in both terms.

activities.label: Chain rule model
activities.title: Chain rule structure
activities.body: Study the rule map, then get ready to explain it back in your own words.

essentialIdeas: Differentiate a composite function by applying the chain rule to the outer and inner parts.

activities.label: Reexplain chain rule
activities.title: Say the chain rule again
activities.body: Explain the chain rule from memory in plain language.
activities.correctAnswer: For a composite function, differentiate the outer function and multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
activities.feedback: A complete answer shows the outside function first and the inside derivative second. If you said only the outside part, add the inner rate as the multiplier.

activities.label: Rule recognition check
activities.title: Choose the matching rule
activities.body: Pick the rule that fits a function made by putting one function inside another.
choices: Apply the chain rule to the outer and inner functions.
Differentiate each piece separately and add the results.
Use the product rule on the two factors.
Subtract the derivative of the inside from the outside derivative.
activities.correctAnswer: Apply the chain rule to the outer and inner functions.
activities.feedback: A composite function needs the outer derivative times the inner derivative. The other choices describe different rules or an incorrect operation.

targetAssignments.essentialIdea: Differentiate a product by using the product rule on the two function factors.
Differentiate a composite function by applying the chain rule to the outer and inner parts.

items.essentialIdea: Product rule differentiates a product as first times derivative of second plus second times derivative of first.

check.title: Differentiate a product
check.prompt: How do you differentiate the product of two functions f and g?
check.referenceAnswer: Differentiate fg as f g' + g f'.
check.feedback: The derivative splits into two terms, one for each factor.

items.essentialIdea: Chain rule differentiates a composite by multiplying the outer derivative by the inner derivative.

check.title: Differentiate a composite
check.prompt: How do you differentiate a composite function like f(g(x))?
check.referenceAnswer: Differentiate the outer function at the inner function, then multiply by g'(x).
check.feedback: The outer derivative is evaluated first, then multiplied by the inner derivative.

recognitionCheck.title: Pick the chain rule
recognitionCheck.prompt: Which derivative rule applies to f(g(x))?
choices: Differentiate the outer function at the inner function, then multiply by the inner derivative.
Differentiate each factor and add the results.
Differentiate only the inner function and ignore the outer function.
Multiply the function by its derivative.
recognitionCheck.correctAnswer: Differentiate the outer function at the inner function, then multiply by the inner derivative.
recognitionCheck.feedback: That is the chain rule because it links outer and inner derivatives.

activities.body: Answer in Spanish with one sentence. Then restate the pattern in plain words.

activities.correctAnswer: A present-tense question asks when a daily activity happens, and the answer is one complete present-tense sentence about the routine.

items.essentialIdea: Prewar European alliances split powers into Triple Entente and Triple Alliance blocs.

check.title: Alliance blocs before war
check.prompt: How did prewar European alliances divide the major powers?
check.referenceAnswer: They divided the major powers into the Triple Entente and the Triple Alliance blocs.
check.feedback: The key point is the two opposing alliance blocs, not a single general alliance system.

items.essentialIdea: The Sarajevo assassination triggered Austria-Hungary's ultimatum, then Serbia, then wider war.

check.title: From assassination to war
check.prompt: What sequence followed the Sarajevo assassination before the war widened?
check.referenceAnswer: Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia, Serbia responded, and the conflict widened into war.
check.feedback: The sequence matters: assassination first, then ultimatum, then responses and escalation.

items.essentialIdea: 1914 began the war, and 1918 ended it with the armistice.

check.title: War start and end
check.prompt: Which years mark the start and end of World War I?
check.referenceAnswer: World War I began in 1914 and ended in 1918 with the armistice.
check.feedback: Use the start and end years together; 1918 is tied to the armistice ending the fighting.

recognitionCheck.title: Identify the war's end year
recognitionCheck.prompt: Which year ended World War I with the armistice?
recognitionCheck.feedback: 1918 is the armistice year that ended the fighting.

items.essentialIdea: Prewar European alliances and tensions split powers into hostile, militarized blocs.

check.title: Alliance divisions
check.prompt: How did prewar European alliances and tensions shape the political landscape before World War I?
check.referenceAnswer: They divided Europe into hostile, militarized alliance blocs, increasing suspicion and the risk that a local crisis would spread.
check.feedback: The key link is that alliances turned rivalry into two opposed blocs and raised the chance of wider war.

items.essentialIdea: The Sarajevo assassination triggered Austria-Hungary's ultimatum and the war declarations that followed.

check.title: After Sarajevo
check.prompt: What chain of events followed the Sarajevo assassination?
check.referenceAnswer: The assassination led Austria-Hungary to issue an ultimatum to Serbia, then to declare war, which set off further declarations by other powers.
check.feedback: Focus on the immediate escalation from assassination to ultimatum to war declarations.

items.essentialIdea: From 1914 to 1918, World War I moved from rapid expansion to armistice in 1918.

check.title: War ends in 1918
check.prompt: What is the basic chronology from 1914 to 1918 in World War I?
check.referenceAnswer: World War I began in 1914 and ended with the 1918 armistice.
check.feedback: The important point is the war's span from outbreak in 1914 to armistice in 1918.

recognitionCheck.title: War outbreak sequence
recognitionCheck.prompt: Which event came first in the outbreak sequence?
choices: The Sarajevo assassination
The 1918 armistice
The end of World War I in 1918
The signing of the armistice after four years of war
recognitionCheck.feedback: The assassination was the starting event; the other choices describe later war outcomes.
